title: Med Spa Package Refund Policy: What to Do With Unused Sessions (October 2026)
summary: Write a med spa package refund policy that covers contraindications, expiry and credit conversion, with the exact steps for handling an unused package.
body_markdown:
## What a Med Spa Package Refund Policy Has to Cover


A med spa package refund policy has to answer five questions in plain language: how long the package is valid, whether it can be refunded and when, what happens to unused value, what happens if the clinic stops the treatment for a safety reason, and who can approve an exception. Everything else is detail.


Published clinic policies show how much room there is inside those five answers. One clinic states that[prepaid packages expire 12 months after purchase and cannot be refunded](https://www.cosmeticare.com/refund-and-return-policy) , though unused sessions can go toward other services at a prorated value. Another allows[refunds of unused packages within 14 days of purchase](https://eclipsespa.odoo.com/return-and-refund-policy) as long as no treatment has been redeemed. Both are defensible. What is not defensible is having neither written down.


Keep the policy to one page and have the patient sign it at purchase, the same way they sign consents. Our guide to[med spa consent forms](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-consent-forms) covers how to store signed documents so they are in the chart when a dispute starts.


## Credit, Prorated Value or Cash: Choosing Your Default


For most clinics the safest default is credit for the remaining value, with cash refunds limited to a short window after purchase or to cases where the clinic cancels the service. Credit keeps the revenue in the business, and the patient still gets full value from what they paid.


Option What the patient gets Good for Watch out for


Cash refund within a short window Money back to the card if no treatment has been used Buyer's remorse in the first days Needs a clear cutoff, such as 14 days, and a "nothing redeemed" condition


Credit for remaining value Balance usable on any service or product Contraindications, changed plans, long gaps Decide whether credit expires and whether it is transferable


Prorated value toward a different treatment Unused sessions swapped to another service at a computed value Patients who still want to be treated, just not with this protocol Needs the formula written down so staff do not guess


No refund, no credit Nothing after treatment begins Almost never the right default Highest dispute and chargeback risk when the stop was not the patient's choice


The strict version still shows up. One policy counts a package as delivered once it has begun, and another says[patients ruled out at the good faith exam should never be penalized](https://medspastandards.com/blog/med-spa-cancellation-no-show-policy-template) . That second principle is the one to build on: the reason a patient cannot finish matters.


## When a Contraindication Stops the Package


When a provider stops a package for a clinical reason, treat the unused value as the patient's to keep, usually as credit, because the patient did not choose to skip the sessions. This is the case that sends front desks to the owner, and it is the one most policies forget to mention.


A realistic version: a patient buys a microneedling and peel package for $900. At the first appointment she mentions a medication that rules out both treatments. Nothing was delivered. A clinic that applies a flat "no refunds on packages" rule here is asking for a bad review or a card dispute over a decision the clinic itself made for safety reasons.


Handle it in this order:


1. The provider documents the contraindication and the decision in the chart, in the same note as the visit.
2. The front desk checks the package agreement for the remedy the policy promises.
3. The approver (owner or practice manager) confirms the remaining value using the formula below.
4. The package is closed out and the value is moved to the patient's account as credit, or refunded if your policy says so for clinic-initiated stops.
5. The patient gets a short written confirmation of the amount and what it can be used for.


Screening that catches contraindications before the money changes hands avoids most of these. Intake questions for medications and conditions belong in the booking flow, which our post on[patient screening at intake](https://decodahealth.com/blog/glp1-trt-peptide-patient-screening-intake) walks through.


## How to Calculate the Value of Unused Sessions


Calculate unused value from what the patient paid, not from the menu price: take the amount paid, subtract the share consumed by delivered sessions at their proportion of the package's full-price value, and the remainder is what the patient is owed. Using list price for the sessions that were used, but the discounted price for the ones that were not, shorts the patient or the clinic depending on which way you round.


Take a three-session package with a full-price value of $1,200, sold for $900. The patient completes one session, which carries a full-price value of $400.


Step Calculation Result


Package paid Amount the patient paid $900


Share consumed $400 of $1,200 full-price value 33.3%


Value consumed at paid price 33.3% of $900 $300


Remaining value $900 minus $300 $600


The alternative, charging the full $400 list price for the delivered session and returning $500, penalizes the patient for the discount they were sold. Whichever method you pick, state it in the agreement, because the CosmetiCare policy shows this is where wording matters: its terms calculate prorated value[from the full retail price of completed treatments](https://www.cosmeticare.com/refund-and-return-policy) .


Taxes and processing fees complicate the number when a package was paid in several charges. Refund against the specific package, never the entire payment, because one payment can cover products and other items as well.


## Expiration Windows and How to Warn Patients


A package expiration window should be stated before purchase, tracked in your system, and reinforced by a reminder well before the end date. Published policies run from 12 months to two years, and one clinic's terms say[unused sessions can be redeemed only if the package has not expired](https://www.cosmeticare.com/refund-and-return-policy) .


Expiry works against you if it surprises people. A patient who learns on the day of the visit that last month's expiry killed a $600 balance will dispute it, and you will usually lose the argument for goodwill even if you win it on paper. Send reminders at 90 and 30 days, and make a rebooking link part of the message. Our post on[med spa retention and rebooking](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-retention-and-rebooking) covers the reminder cadence that brings patients back.


State law is the main constraint on expiry and cash redemption. The CosmetiCare policy, for example, cites California's gift certificate statute,[Civil Code section 1749.5](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1749.5) , to explain why it treats packages as service agreements rather than gift certificates. Whether that logic holds in your state is a question for your attorney, not for your front desk.


## Where Unused Package Money Sits on Your Books


Money collected for sessions you have not delivered is a liability until you perform the service or close the package, so an unused package is not revenue yet. Converting it to credit does not erase the liability. It moves it from the package to the patient's balance.


That has a practical effect on cash planning. A clinic that sells a lot of packages in the fourth quarter carries a large undelivered balance into January, which our post on[med spa seasonal cash flow](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-seasonal-cash-flow-planning) works through with numbers. It also means a weekly look at unapplied package balances belongs in your close routine, next to the checks in the[med spa KPI guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-kpi-tracking) .


Operators moving from another system tell us the same story: packages are the part that does not survive a migration cleanly, and some clinics keep running the old point of sale for months because of it. Our write-up on[what transfers in a med spa EMR migration](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-emr-migration-what-transfers) explains what to check before you commit.


## Handling the Request at the Front Desk Without Calling the Owner


Staff should be able to resolve the common cases without an escalation by following a short decision table that matches the policy. The goal is that two patients in the same situation get the same answer, whoever they speak to.


Situation Default remedy Who approves


Within the refund window, nothing used Refund to original card Front desk


Provider stops treatment for a clinical reason Credit for remaining value (or refund, if your policy says so) Practice manager


Patient moves away or changes plans mid-package Credit for remaining value, per policy Front desk, within the formula


Package expired Follow the written rule; owner discretion for goodwill Owner


Dispute over results Not a package question; follow the treatment policy Owner or medical director


The thing to protect is the audit trail. Whatever the remedy, the note should record who approved it, the amount and the reason. That record is what you show a processor or a state board if the patient escalates.

## Final Thoughts on Your Med Spa Package Refund Policy


Write the rule before the first awkward patient asks for it. Default to credit, carve out the clinical-stop case, put the valuation formula in the agreement and have an attorney read it for your state. ## Frequently Asked Questions


Do med spas have to refund unused packages?


It depends on your written terms and your state's consumer law, so there is no single federal answer. Most clinics offer credit or a prorated value instead of cash once treatment has begun, and some refund in full within a short window after purchase. Put your rule in the package agreement the patient signs, and ask a healthcare attorney to review it for your state.


What should a med spa do when a patient cannot finish a package because of a contraindication?


Document the contraindication in the chart, then offer a remedy your policy already promises, usually credit for the unused value toward other services or products. A patient who is turned away for a safety reason did not choose to skip the sessions, so a strict no-refund clause applied to them reads as unfair and invites disputes. Decide the remedy once, in writing, before it happens.


How do you calculate the value of an unused package?


Divide what the patient paid by the full-price value of the package, then subtract the full retail price of the sessions already delivered. A $900 package with one of three sessions used at full price of $400 leaves the remaining value after that $400, scaled by the discount the patient received. Write the formula into your policy so staff never improvise it at the front desk.


Should a med spa refund unused packages as cash or as credit?


Credit is the more common choice, because the clinic keeps the revenue and the patient keeps the value. Cash refunds are usually reserved for a short window after purchase, for cases where the clinic cancels the service, or where the law requires it. Whichever you pick, say so in the agreement and apply it the same way to every patient.


Can a med spa package expire?


Many do, commonly after 12 to 24 months, and published clinic policies show windows from one year to two. Expiration terms must be disclosed before purchase, and some states restrict them, so confirm yours with counsel. Track the expiry date in your system and warn patients 60 to 90 days ahead so an expiry never comes as a surprise.


How should unused package money be recorded on the books?


Money collected for sessions not yet delivered is a liability, not earned revenue, until the service is performed or the package is cancelled. When you convert a package to credit, the liability moves from the package to the patient's credit balance rather than disappearing. Ask your bookkeeper to confirm the treatment for your entity and state.
